claim: PPP1R35 was previously identified in fractions co-purifying with centrosomes in a high-throughput mass spectrometry study.
source: PPP1R35, the product of the gene C7orf47, which was previously identified in fractions co-purifying with centrosomes in a high-throughput mass spectrometry study (Jakobsen et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Jakobsen et al., 2011, which is a reference to prior published work.

claim: PPP1R35 is a centrosomal component located in the proximal centriolar lumen above the cartwheel.
source: Our study demonstrates that PPP1R35 is a centrosomal component located in the proximal centriolar lumen above the cartwheel.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from super-resolution microscopy mapping and live-cell imaging presented in the manuscript.

claim: PPP1R35 is not important for early centriole assembly but is critical for centriole elongation.
source: We further demonstrate that PPP1R35 is not important for early centriole assembly but is critical for centriole elongation by impacting the recruitment of the microtubule-binding elongation machinery.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from siRNA knockdown experiments and immunofluorescence analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: PPP1R35 acts downstream of RTTN in the elongation pathway.
source: In addition, we show that PPP1R35 is downstream of RTTN in the elongation pathway and that they form a protein complex.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from BioID, immunoprecipitation, and recruitment assays presented in the manuscript.

claim: PPP1R35 forms a protein complex with RTTN.
source: In addition, we show that PPP1R35 is downstream of RTTN in the elongation pathway and that they form a protein complex.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from BioID and FLAG immunoprecipitation experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: GFP-PPP1R35 co-localizes with Centrin 1-mCherry at centrosomes.
source: To verify that the observed PPP1R35 was located at the centrosomes, we transfected the GFP-PPP1R35 U2OS Flp-In cell line with a vector expressing Centrin 1-mCherry and observed co-localization of Centrin 1-mCherry with GFP-PPP1R35 (Figure 1a).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy imaging data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: PPP1R35 is found on two centrosomes (grandmother and mother) throughout the entire cell cycle.
source: PPP1R35 was found on two centrosomes (grandmother and mother) throughout the entire cell cycle (Figure 1b).
evidence: The claim is supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 1b and Video 1.

claim: PPP1R35 is recruited on daughter centrioles prior to mitosis.
source: We observed some cells that have four GFP-PPP1R35 spots prior to mitosis (Video 1) and noted that a second GFP-PPP1R35 spot was always present after mitosis, suggesting that PPP1R35 is recruited on daughter centrioles prior to mitosis.
evidence: The claim is supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Video 1 and is based on inference from the observation of four spots prior to mitosis.

claim: PPP1R35 resides on both the mother and daughter centrioles in G2 cells.
source: In all G2 cells examined, prior to centrosome separation, two GFP-PPP1R35 spots are resolvable on each of the centrioles (grandmother and mother), confirming that PPP1R35 resides on both the mother and daughter centrioles and must be recruited early in the duplication cycle, in S or early G2 phase (Figure 1c).
evidence: The claim is supported by sub-diffraction live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: PPP1R35 must be recruited early in the duplication cycle, in S or early G2 phase.
source: In all G2 cells examined, prior to centrosome separation, two GFP-PPP1R35 spots are resolvable on each of the centrioles (grandmother and mother), confirming that PPP1R35 resides on both the mother and daughter centrioles and must be recruited early in the duplication cycle, in S or early G2 phase (Figure 1c).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that PPP1R35 is present on both mother and daughter centrioles in G2 cells.

claim: Endogenous PPP1R35 co-localizes with γ-tubulin at centrosomes.
source: To confirm that GFP-PPP1R35 localization is consistent with the endogenous protein, we imaged U2OS cells labeled with antibodies against PPP1R35 and γ-tubulin by confocal microscopy (Figure 1d) and cells labeled with antibodies against PPP1R35 and CETN1 by 3D structured illumination microscopy (3DSIM), and observed co-localization (Figure 1e).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy imaging data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: Endogenous PPP1R35 co-localizes with CETN1 at centrosomes.
source: To confirm that GFP-PPP1R35 localization is consistent with the endogenous protein, we imaged U2OS cells labeled with antibodies against PPP1R35 and γ-tubulin by confocal microscopy (Figure 1d) and cells labeled with antibodies against PPP1R35 and CETN1 by 3D structured illumination microscopy (3DSIM), and observed co-localization (Figure 1e).
evidence: The claim is supported by 3DSIM imaging data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: The GFP tag does not impact the localization of PPP1R35.
source: To ensure that the GFP tag did not impact the localization of the protein, we examined the morphology of the centrosome by 3DSIM and did not observe a difference between WT and GFP-PPP1R35-expressing U2OS cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: The claim is supported by 3DSIM imaging data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a.

claim: The GFP-PPP1R35 construct does not alter centrosome biogenesis.
source: Furthermore, we verified that the GFP-PPP1R35 construct did not alter centrosome biogenesis by measuring the total number of CEP152-labeled centrosomes in WT and GFP-PPP1R35-expressing U2OS cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of CEP152-labeled centrosomes shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b.

claim: The GFP-PPP1R35 construct rescues the centriole duplication phenotype when PPP1R35 levels are knocked down by siRNA targeting the 3' untranslated region.
source: In addition, the GFP-PPP1R35 construct rescues the centriole duplication phenotype when PPP1R35 levels are knocked down by siRNA targeting the 3' untranslated region (3'UTR, see below Figure 3c).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Centrosomal PPP1R35 has low turnover and is stably associated at the centrosome.
source: Comparison of the fluorescence recovery curves of the cytoplasmic versus centrosomal PPP1R35 pools revealed that centrosomal PPP1R35 did not fully recover to pre-bleach levels after photobleaching, therefore indicating that the protein has low turnover and is stably associated at the centrosome (Figure 1f,g).
evidence: The claim is supported by FRAP experimental data shown in Figure 1f,g.

claim: Only 22% turnover in centrosomal PPP1R35 was measured by SILAC mass spectrometry.
source: This observation is consistent with a previous analysis that identified PPP1R35 as co-purifying with centrosomal components and observed only a 22% turnover in centrosomal PPP1R35 as measured by stable isotope labeling of amino acids in cell culture (SILAC) mass spectrometry (Jakobsen et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Jakobsen et al., 2011, which is a reference to prior published work.

claim: PPP1R35 is located in the centrosomal lumen.
source: 3DSIM imaging showed that GFP-PPP1R35 is located in the centrosomal lumen, as suggested by the position of PPP1R35 in the middle of the ring structure formed by CEP152 (Hatch et al., 2010; Cizmecioglu et al., 2010) (Figure 2a).
evidence: The claim is supported by 3DSIM imaging data shown in Figure 2a and is consistent with the known localization of CEP152.

claim: PPP1R35 is located 230 ± 50 nm from Centrin-1.
source: 3DSIM molecular mapping shows that PPP1R35 is located furthest from the distal end proteins (Centrin-1: 230 ± 50 nm; POC5: 160 ± 50 nm; POC1B: 140 ± 60 nm), but closer to proximal end markers such as CEP135 (90 ± 40 nm) and CPAP (60 ± 30 nm), yet not as proximal as SAS6 (120 ± 40 nm) or CEP250 (170 ± 50 nm) (Figure 2d).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative 3DSIM molecular mapping data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: PPP1R35 is located 160 ± 50 nm from POC5.
source: 3DSIM molecular mapping shows that PPP1R35 is located furthest from the distal end proteins (Centrin-1: 230 ± 50 nm; POC5: 160 ± 50 nm; POC1B: 140 ± 60 nm), but closer to proximal end markers such as CEP135 (90 ± 40 nm) and CPAP (60 ± 30 nm), yet not as proximal as SAS6 (120 ± 40 nm) or CEP250 (170 ± 50 nm) (Figure 2d).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative 3DSIM molecular mapping data shown in Figure 2d.

evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative 3DSIM molecular mapping data shown in Figure 2d.

evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative 3DSIM molecular mapping data shown in Figure 2d.

evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative 3DSIM molecular mapping data shown in Figure 2d.

evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative 3DSIM molecular mapping data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: PPP1R35 localizes to the proximal centriolar lumen just above the cartwheel.
source: Together, we conclude that PPP1R35 localizes to the proximal centriolar lumen just above the cartwheel (Figure 2e).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative 3DSIM molecular mapping data shown in Figure 2d and summarized in Figure 2e.

claim: Depletion of PPP1R35 by siRNA results in a significant decrease in centrosomal staining of CEP152.
source: With both siRNA strands, a significant decrease was observed in centrosomal staining of CEP152, a protein recruited in the last stages of daughter centriole formation (Fu et al., 2016)(Figure 3c).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from siRNA knockdown experiments shown in Figure 3c.

claim: CEP152 is a protein recruited in the last stages of daughter centriole formation.
source: With both siRNA strands, a significant decrease was observed in centrosomal staining of CEP152, a protein recruited in the last stages of daughter centriole formation (Fu et al., 2016)(Figure 3c).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Fu et al., 2016, which is a reference to prior published work.

claim: Centriolar components recruited early in the pathway such as SAS6, CEP135 and Centrin 1 are modestly affected at centrioles in the absence of PPP1R35.
source: This analysis revealed that centriolar components recruited early in the pathway such as SAS6 (Dzhindzhev et al., 2014), CEP135 (Loncarek and Bettencourt-Dias, 2018; Fu et al., 2015) and Centrin 1 (Middendorp et al., 1997), are modestly affected at centrioles in the absence of PPP1R35, as opposed to proteins recruited in later stages, such as CEP295 (Chang et al., 2016), POC1B (Venoux et al., 2013), and CEP152 (Loncarek and Bettencourt-Dias, 2018; Fu et al., 2015) that are drastically reduced (Figure 3e and Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from siRNA knockdown experiments shown in Figure 3e and Figure 3—figure supplement 4, and by citations to prior published work.

claim: Proteins recruited in later stages of centriole duplication, such as CEP295, POC1B, and CEP152, are drastically reduced in the absence of PPP1R35.
source: This analysis revealed that centriolar components recruited early in the pathway such as SAS6 (Dzhindzhev et al., 2014), CEP135 (Loncarek and Bettencourt-Dias, 2018; Fu et al., 2015) and Centrin 1 (Middendorp et al., 1997), are modestly affected at centrioles in the absence of PPP1R35, as opposed to proteins recruited in later stages, such as CEP295 (Chang et al., 2016), POC1B (Venoux et al., 2013), and CEP152 (Loncarek and Bettencourt-Dias, 2018; Fu et al., 2015) that are drastically reduced (Figure 3e and Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from siRNA knockdown experiments shown in Figure 3e and Figure 3—figure supplement 4, and by citations to prior published work.

claim: PPP1R35 knockdown results in a significant reduction in Cdk5rap2 at centrosomes.
source: To assay for centrosome function, we examined whether centrosomes could recruit the pericentriolar material or efficiently nucleate microtubules in the absence of PPP1R35 by staining for Cdk5rap2 and γ-tubulin. In both cases, we observed a significant reduction upon PPP1R35 knockdown (Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from siRNA knockdown experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claim: PPP1R35 knockdown results in a significant reduction in γ-tubulin at centrosomes.
source: To assay for centrosome function, we examined whether centrosomes could recruit the pericentriolar material or efficiently nucleate microtubules in the absence of PPP1R35 by staining for Cdk5rap2 and γ-tubulin. In both cases, we observed a significant reduction upon PPP1R35 knockdown (Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from siRNA knockdown experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claim: The proportion of engaged centrosomes with cartwheels is not significantly different when cells are treated with PPP1R35 siRNA.
source: When cells treated with PPP1R35 siRNA were stained for CEP152 and SAS6, the proportion of engaged centrosomes with cartwheels was not significantly different (Figure 3g), further suggesting that PPP1R35 loss does not influence the early stages of centriole biogenesis.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from siRNA knockdown experiments shown in Figure 3g.

claim: PPP1R35 loss does not influence the early stages of centriole biogenesis.
source: When cells treated with PPP1R35 siRNA were stained for CEP152 and SAS6, the proportion of engaged centrosomes with cartwheels was not significantly different (Figure 3g), further suggesting that PPP1R35 loss does not influence the early stages of centriole biogenesis.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that cartwheel formation is not significantly affected by PPP1R35 knockdown.

claim: At longer timepoints (>72hr) after PPP1R35 knockdown, CETN1 levels drastically decrease.
source: It is also noteworthy that at longer timepoints (>72hr), CETN1 levels drastically decrease suggesting that overall centriole formation is being impacted.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from time-course siRNA knockdown experiments.

claim: PPP1R35 loss of function results in decreased centrosome number.
source: Altogether, these results demonstrate that PPP1R35 loss of function results in decreased centrosome number and suggest that PPP1R35 is critical for the recruitment of centriolar components after cartwheel formation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from siRNA knockdown experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: PPP1R35 is critical for the recruitment of centriolar components after cartwheel formation.
source: Altogether, these results demonstrate that PPP1R35 loss of function results in decreased centrosome number and suggest that PPP1R35 is critical for the recruitment of centriolar components after cartwheel formation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that early centriolar components are modestly affected while later components are drastically reduced upon PPP1R35 knockdown.

claim: RTTN is one of the most robust hits in the PPP1R35 BioID proximity map.
source: One of the most robust hits, as evidenced by the high numbers of peptides identified by both N- and C-terminal BirA* tags, is RTTN, a recently characterized protein (H.-Y. Chen et al., 2017) whose mutations in patients cause microcephaly (Care4Rare Canada Consortium et al., 2015; Grandone et al., 2016), dwarfism, and polymicrogyria (Kheradmand Kia et al., 2012) (Figure 4a; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by BioID experimental data shown in Figure 4a and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Mutations in RTTN cause microcephaly in patients.
source: One of the most robust hits, as evidenced by the high numbers of peptides identified by both N- and C-terminal BirA* tags, is RTTN, a recently characterized protein (H.-Y. Chen et al., 2017) whose mutations in patients cause microcephaly (Care4Rare Canada Consortium et al., 2015; Grandone et al., 2016), dwarfism, and polymicrogyria (Kheradmand Kia et al., 2012) (Figure 4a; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Care4Rare Canada Consortium et al., 2015 and Grandone et al., 2016, which are references to prior published work.

claim: Mutations in RTTN cause dwarfism in patients.
source: One of the most robust hits, as evidenced by the high numbers of peptides identified by both N- and C-terminal BirA* tags, is RTTN, a recently characterized protein (H.-Y. Chen et al., 2017) whose mutations in patients cause microcephaly (Care4Rare Canada Consortium et al., 2015; Grandone et al., 2016), dwarfism, and polymicrogyria (Kheradmand Kia et al., 2012) (Figure 4a; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kheradmand Kia et al., 2012, which is a reference to prior published work.

claim: Mutations in RTTN cause polymicrogyria in patients.
source: One of the most robust hits, as evidenced by the high numbers of peptides identified by both N- and C-terminal BirA* tags, is RTTN, a recently characterized protein (H.-Y. Chen et al., 2017) whose mutations in patients cause microcephaly (Care4Rare Canada Consortium et al., 2015; Grandone et al., 2016), dwarfism, and polymicrogyria (Kheradmand Kia et al., 2012) (Figure 4a; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kheradmand Kia et al., 2012, which is a reference to prior published work.

claim: RTTN was found to form a complex with the N-terminally tagged BirA*-PPP1R35.
source: Notably, RTTN was found to form a complex with the N-terminally tagged BirA*-PPP1R35.
evidence: The claim is supported by FLAG immunoprecipitation experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: RTTN was the only protein identified with high confidence by BioID that also co-immunoprecipitated with PPP1R35.
source: RTTN was the only protein identified with high confidence by BioID that also co-immunoprecipitated with PPP1R35, suggesting a strong link between this microcephaly protein and PPP1R35 function.
evidence: The claim is supported by BioID and FLAG immunoprecipitation experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: IP-mass spectrometry data using the N-terminal FLAG-tagged PPP1R35 detected a high-confidence interaction with RTTN.
source: Interestingly, IP-mass spectrometry data using the N-terminal FLAG-tagged PPP1R35, but not the C-terminal FLAG-tag construct, detected a high-confidence interaction with RTTN.
evidence: The claim is supported by FLAG immunoprecipitation mass spectrometry experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: IP with the PPP1R35 C-terminal FLAG-tag construct identified RTTN peptide counts above that of the controls, but below the confidence level cut-off.
source: IP with the PPP1R35 C-terminal FLAG-tag construct still identified RTTN peptide counts above that of the controls, but below our confidence level cut-off (Supplementary file 1), indicating that the interaction between the two proteins has been severely impaired but not completely abolished.
evidence: The claim is supported by FLAG immunoprecipitation mass spectrometry experimental data presented in Supplementary file 1.

claim: The binding site between PPP1R35 and RTTN might reside within the conserved C-terminal region of PPP1R35.
source: Altogether, this suggests that the binding site might reside within the conserved C-terminal region of PPP1R35.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that the C-terminal FLAG-tag impairs the interaction with RTTN.

claim: RTTN localizes to the proximal centriole.
source: Our data show that RTTN localizes to the proximal centriole and it is located in close proximity to PPP1R35, consistent with our BioID findings (PPP1R35 distance from mCherry-RTTN, 80 ± 50 nm; anti-RTTN, 110 ± 50 nm; Figure 4d).
evidence: The claim is supported by 3DSIM imaging and quantitative analysis shown in Figure 4d.

claim: RTTN is located in close proximity to PPP1R35.
source: Our data show that RTTN localizes to the proximal centriole and it is located in close proximity to PPP1R35, consistent with our BioID findings (PPP1R35 distance from mCherry-RTTN, 80 ± 50 nm; anti-RTTN, 110 ± 50 nm; Figure 4d).
evidence: The claim is supported by 3DSIM imaging and quantitative analysis shown in Figure 4d.

claim: PPP1R35 is located 80 ± 50 nm from mCherry-RTTN.
source: Our data show that RTTN localizes to the proximal centriole and it is located in close proximity to PPP1R35, consistent with our BioID findings (PPP1R35 distance from mCherry-RTTN, 80 ± 50 nm; anti-RTTN, 110 ± 50 nm; Figure 4d).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative 3DSIM molecular mapping data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: PPP1R35 is located 110 ± 50 nm from anti-RTTN antibody signal.
source: Our data show that RTTN localizes to the proximal centriole and it is located in close proximity to PPP1R35, consistent with our BioID findings (PPP1R35 distance from mCherry-RTTN, 80 ± 50 nm; anti-RTTN, 110 ± 50 nm; Figure 4d).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative 3DSIM molecular mapping data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: The presence of RTTN at the centrosome is moderately, yet significantly, diminished upon PPP1R35 depletion.
source: The presence of RTTN at the centrosome is moderately, yet significantly, diminished upon PPP1R35 depletion (Figure 4e).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from siRNA knockdown experiments shown in Figure 4e.

claim: A major reduction in centrosomal PPP1R35 is observed when RTTN is depleted.
source: When the reciprocal recruitment was explored by RTTN depletion, a major reduction in centrosomal PPP1R35 was observed (Figure 4f).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from siRNA knockdown experiments shown in Figure 4f.

claim: The number of cells with at least 2 centrin spots remains unchanged upon RTTN knockdown.
source: This phenotype appears to be unrelated to the decrease in centriole number expected as a result of RTTN knockdown (Chen et al., 2017), because the number of cells with at least 2 centrin spots remains unchanged (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), yet the number of cells lacking GFP-PPP1R35 is significantly reduced.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: RTTN and PPP1R35 co-localize at the centriole.
source: These results show that the two proteins co-localize at the centriole and that both proteins are mutually required for each other's recruitment to the centriole, with RTTN exerting a more significant impact on PPP1R35 recruitment to the centriole.
evidence: The claim is supported by 3DSIM imaging and recruitment assay data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Both PPP1R35 and RTTN are mutually required for each other's recruitment to the centriole.
source: These results show that the two proteins co-localize at the centriole and that both proteins are mutually required for each other's recruitment to the centriole, with RTTN exerting a more significant impact on PPP1R35 recruitment to the centriole.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from reciprocal siRNA knockdown experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: RTTN exerts a more significant impact on PPP1R35 recruitment to the centriole than PPP1R35 does on RTTN recruitment.
source: These results show that the two proteins co-localize at the centriole and that both proteins are mutually required for each other's recruitment to the centriole, with RTTN exerting a more significant impact on PPP1R35 recruitment to the centriole.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from reciprocal siRNA knockdown experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: RTTN acts upstream of PPP1R35.
source: Altogether, our data suggest that RTTN and PPP1R35 form a complex and that RTTN acts upstream of PPP1R35.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that RTTN depletion has a more significant impact on PPP1R35 recruitment than vice versa.

claim: PPP1R35 is a highly conserved protein whose homologs are found across a wide range of eukaryotic species.
source: PPP1R35 is a highly conserved protein whose homologs are found across a wide range of eukaryotic species, ranging from the simple multicellular organism Trichoplax adhaerens to Homo sapiens (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: PPP1R35 homologues are found only in Holozoa species.
source: Interestingly, PPP1R35 homologues are found only in Holozoa species, correlating well with species presenting centrosomes, with the exception of Caenorhabditis elegans (Hodges et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis and is consistent with the known distribution of centrosomes across species.

claim: PPP1R35 can be divided into two major domains based on amino acid sequence homology: the highly divergent N-terminal domain and the more conserved C-terminal domain.
source: PPP1R35 can be divided into two major domains based on amino acid sequence homology: the highly divergent N-terminal domain and the more conserved C-terminal domain (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The N-terminus of PPP1R35 contains several highly conserved residues in mammalian species including three serine residues (S45, S47, S52 in Homo sapiens PPP1R35).
source: Despite its variability across evolution, the N-terminus contains several highly conserved residues in mammalian species including three serine residues (S45, S47, S52 in Homo sapiens PPP1R35) previously found phosphorylated in large scale phospho-proteomic studies in both human and mouse cells (Olsen et al., 2010; Dephoure et al., 2008; Chi et al., 2008) (Figure 5a and Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment analysis and citations to prior published work.

claim: S45, S47, and S52 in PPP1R35 were previously found phosphorylated in large scale phospho-proteomic studies in both human and mouse cells.
source: Despite its variability across evolution, the N-terminus contains several highly conserved residues in mammalian species including three serine residues (S45, S47, S52 in Homo sapiens PPP1R35) previously found phosphorylated in large scale phospho-proteomic studies in both human and mouse cells (Olsen et al., 2010; Dephoure et al., 2008; Chi et al., 2008) (Figure 5a and Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Olsen et al., 2010; Dephoure et al., 2008; Chi et al., 2008, which are references to prior published work.

claim: S47 and S52 in PPP1R35 have been reported to be Cdk phosphorylation sites.
source: In particular, S47 and S52 have been reported to be Cdk phosphorylation sites (Chi et al., 2008) (Figure 5a).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Chi et al., 2008, which is a reference to prior published work.

claim: Neither the triple alanine nor the triple aspartic acid mutant of PPP1R35 significantly impacted the presence of PPP1R35 at the centrosome.
source: Neither the triple alanine nor the triple aspartic acid mutant significantly impacted the presence of PPP1R35 at the centrosome, nor its proximity to RTTN (Figure 5b,g).
evidence: The claim is supported by BioID and 3DSIM imaging data shown in Figure 5b,g.

claim: Neither the triple alanine nor the triple aspartic acid mutant of PPP1R35 significantly impacted its proximity to RTTN.
source: Neither the triple alanine nor the triple aspartic acid mutant significantly impacted the presence of PPP1R35 at the centrosome, nor its proximity to RTTN (Figure 5b,g).
evidence: The claim is supported by BioID and 3DSIM imaging data shown in Figure 5b,g.

claim: Neither phospho-mutant of PPP1R35 impacted the interaction between PPP1R35 and RTTN.
source: Furthermore, co-IP demonstrated that neither phospho-mutant impacted the interaction between PPP1R35 and RTTN (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: The triple aspartic acid mutant (S45D, S47D, S52D) GFP-PPP1R35 rescues the centriole defect phenotype when endogenous PPP1R35 is depleted.
source: When cells were depleted of endogenous PPP1R35 by the 3' UTR-targeting siRNA and expressed the triple aspartic acid mutant (S45D, S47D, S52D) GFP-PPP1R35 in trans, we did not observe any reduction in centrosome number (Figure 5c).
evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: Individual alanine mutants (S45A and S47A) of PPP1R35 are consistent with the notion that these residues are not playing a critical role in PPP1R35's function in centriole biogenesis.

claim: Disruption of the predicted PP1 binding site by mutating V79 and F81 to alanine leads to proper targeting of PPP1R35 to the centriole.

claim: The length of mother centrioles in control-RNAi treated cells is 356 ± 65 nm.
source: The length of mother centrioles was determined to be 356 ± 65 nm in control-RNAi treated cells, in agreement with previous reports (Thauvin-Robinet et al., 2014).

claim: PPP1R35 knockdown results in a significant reduction in centriole length to 263 ± 69 nm for the exon siRNA.

claim: PPP1R35 knockdown results in a significant reduction in centriole length to 246 ± 83 nm for the 3' UTR siRNA.

claim: Overexpression of PPP1R35 does not significantly change centriole length.
source: On the contrary, overexpression of PPP1R35 does not significantly change centriole length (382 ± 89 nm).
evidence: The claim is supported by 3DSIM centriole length measurement data.

evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from siRNA knockdown experiments and citations to prior published work.

claim: SPICE is significantly reduced in cells treated with PPP1R35 siRNA.
source: We then examined cells treated with PPP1R35 siRNA for recruitment of proteins involved in either microtubule stabilization/recruitment such as CPAP and SPICE (Archinti et al., 2010; Zheng et al., 2016a; Tang et al., 2009; Comartin et al., 2013; Lin et al., 2013b) or the elongation of the distal portion of the centriole such as POC5 (Azimzadeh et al., 2009) and both proteins were significantly reduced in the absence of PPP1R35.

claim: PPP1R35 is a critical factor for centriole assembly by promoting recruitment of centriole elongation proteins.
source: Altogether, this demonstrates that PPP1R35 is a critical factor for centriole assembly by promoting recruitment of centriole elongation proteins.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from siRNA knockdown experiments and centriole length measurements presented in the manuscript.

claim: The centrosome is a membrane-less organelle whose major role is to organize, orient, and regulate the site of microtubule formation.
source: The centrosome is a membrane-less organelle whose major role is to organize, orient, and regulate the site of microtubule formation.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about centrosome function.

claim: In somatic dividing cells, the centrosome is critical for ensuring faithful and timely chromosome segregation and establishment of the correct cell division axis.
source: In somatic dividing cells, the centrosome is critical for ensuring faithful and timely chromosome segregation and establishment of the correct cell division axis, whereas in non-dividing and differentiated cells, it is critical for cellular polarization and cilia formation (Conduit et al., 2015; Vertii et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge and is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: In non-dividing and differentiated cells, the centrosome is critical for cellular polarization and cilia formation.
source: In somatic dividing cells, the centrosome is critical for ensuring faithful and timely chromosome segregation and establishment of the correct cell division axis, whereas in non-dividing and differentiated cells, it is critical for cellular polarization and cilia formation (Conduit et al., 2015; Vertii et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge and is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Centrosomes are essential for normal human development and health.
source: Centrosomes are essential for normal human development and health (Nigg and Holland, 2018).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge and is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: Loss of function mutations in centrosomal proteins are responsible for developmental defects such as primary recessive microcephaly.
source: Loss of function mutations in centrosomal proteins, including components of the centriolar cartwheel, elongation machinery, appendages, and pericentriolar material, are responsible for developmental defects such as primary recessive microcephaly (Barbelanne and Tsang, 2014), primordial dwarfism (Care4Rare Canada Consortium et al., 2015; Rauch et al., 2008; Zheng et al., 2016b), and ciliopathies (Reiter and Leroux, 2017).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge and is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Loss of function mutations in centrosomal proteins are responsible for primordial dwarfism.
source: Loss of function mutations in centrosomal proteins, including components of the centriolar cartwheel, elongation machinery, appendages, and pericentriolar material, are responsible for developmental defects such as primary recessive microcephaly (Barbelanne and Tsang, 2014), primordial dwarfism (Care4Rare Canada Consortium et al., 2015; Rauch et al., 2008; Zheng et al., 2016b), and ciliopathies (Reiter and Leroux, 2017).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge and is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Loss of function mutations in centrosomal proteins are responsible for ciliopathies.
source: Loss of function mutations in centrosomal proteins, including components of the centriolar cartwheel, elongation machinery, appendages, and pericentriolar material, are responsible for developmental defects such as primary recessive microcephaly (Barbelanne and Tsang, 2014), primordial dwarfism (Care4Rare Canada Consortium et al., 2015; Rauch et al., 2008; Zheng et al., 2016b), and ciliopathies (Reiter and Leroux, 2017).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge and is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Defects in centrosome number and structure are a major hallmark of tumorigenesis.
source: Defects in centrosome number and structure are a major hallmark of tumorigenesis (Gönczy, 2015; de Cárcer and Malumbres, 2014; Nigg and Holland, 2018).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge and is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Centrosome over-duplication concomitant with mutations in p53 drives tumor formation in the epidermis in mouse models.
source: Recently, studies in mouse models indicated that centrosome over-duplication concomitant with mutations in p53 drives tumor formation in the epidermis (Serçin et al., 2016) and can drive tumor formation in certain other tissues, even in the absence of concurrent p53-/- mutations (Levine et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Serçin et al., 2016 and Levine et al., 2017, which are references to prior published work.

claim: Centrosome over-duplication can drive tumor formation in certain tissues, even in the absence of concurrent p53-/- mutations.
source: Recently, studies in mouse models indicated that centrosome over-duplication concomitant with mutations in p53 drives tumor formation in the epidermis (Serçin et al., 2016) and can drive tumor formation in certain other tissues, even in the absence of concurrent p53-/- mutations (Levine et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Levine et al., 2017, which is a reference to prior published work.

claim: Centrosome duplication begins in most somatic cells at the G1/S phase boundary with the assembly of the cartwheel.
source: Significant progress has been made in understanding how centrosome duplication begins in most somatic cells—at the G1/S phase boundary—with the assembly of the cartwheel, a nine-fold symmetrical scaffold made of SAS6, STIL, and CEP135.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about centrosome duplication.

claim: The cartwheel is a nine-fold symmetrical scaffold made of SAS6, STIL, and CEP135.
source: Significant progress has been made in understanding how centrosome duplication begins in most somatic cells—at the G1/S phase boundary—with the assembly of the cartwheel, a nine-fold symmetrical scaffold made of SAS6, STIL, and CEP135.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about cartwheel structure.

claim: Plk4 promotes cartwheel formation and centriole duplication by phosphorylating STIL to favor its interaction with SAS6.
source: While SAS6 molecules can undergo remarkable self-assembly in vitro, the kinase Plk4 promotes cartwheel formation and centriole duplication by phosphorylating STIL to favor its interaction with SAS6 (Vulprecht et al., 2012; Lin et al., 2013b; Dzhindzhev et al., 2014; Arquint and Nigg, 2016).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge and is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: The initial binding of Plk4 to the centriole is governed by CEP63, CEP152, and CEP192.
source: The initial binding of Plk4 to the centriole is governed by CEP63 (Brown et al., 2013), CEP152 (Brown et al., 2013; Kim et al., 2013; Sonnen et al., 2013; Dzhindzhev et al., 2010; Hatch et al., 2010; Cizmecioglu et al., 2010), and CEP192 (Kim et al., 2013; Sonnen et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge and is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: CPAP aids in the formation of the centriole microtubule wall after cartwheel formation.
source: After cartwheel formation, CPAP, recruited by STIL (Tang et al., 2011), aids in the formation of the centriole microtubule wall (Pelletier et al., 2006; Schmidt et al., 2009) by regulating centriolar microtubule plus-end dynamics (Basten and Giles, 2013; Zheng et al., 2016a).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge and is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: CPAP is recruited by STIL.
source: After cartwheel formation, CPAP, recruited by STIL (Tang et al., 2011), aids in the formation of the centriole microtubule wall (Pelletier et al., 2006; Schmidt et al., 2009) by regulating centriolar microtubule plus-end dynamics (Basten and Giles, 2013; Zheng et al., 2016a).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge and is supported by a citation to Tang et al., 2011, which is a reference to prior published work.

claim: CEP135 facilitates the stabilization of the centriole structure.
source: CEP135 facilitates the stabilization of the centriole structure (Ohta et al., 2002; Basten and Giles, 2013) but may also play a more direct role in initial cartwheel formation as recombinant Drosophila SAS6 and Bld10 (Drosophila CEP135 homolog) can self-organize into a nine-fold symmetrical cartwheel structure (Guichard et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge and is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Recombinant Drosophila SAS6 and Bld10 can self-organize into a nine-fold symmetrical cartwheel structure.
source: CEP135 facilitates the stabilization of the centriole structure (Ohta et al., 2002; Basten and Giles, 2013) but may also play a more direct role in initial cartwheel formation as recombinant Drosophila SAS6 and Bld10 (Drosophila CEP135 homolog) can self-organize into a nine-fold symmetrical cartwheel structure (Guichard et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Guichard et al., 2017, which is a reference to prior published work.

claim: Centriole elongation happens between S and G2 phases.
source: However, we have a limited understanding of the essential components required for centriole elongation, which happens between S and G2 phases, and how they are assembled in a stepwise manner.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about the cell cycle timing of centriole elongation.

claim: CPAP has been shown to interact with CEP120 and SPICE in a complex that regulates centriole elongation at the centriolar microtubule wall.
source: CPAP has been shown to interact with CEP120 (Lin et al., 2013a) and SPICE (Comartin et al., 2013) in a complex that regulates centriole elongation at the centriolar microtubule wall (Archinti et al., 2010; Lin et al., 2013b).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge and is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Centrobin has been implicated in directly regulating centriolar microtubule elongation and stability.
source: Centrobin has also been implicated in directly regulating centriolar microtubule elongation (Lee et al., 2010; Zou et al., 2005) and stability by binding to α-Tubulin (Gudi et al., 2011) and by regulating CPAP levels (Gudi et al., 2015; Gudi et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge and is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Centrobin is required to recruit CP110.
source: Centrobin is further required to recruit CP110, a protein forming a cap-like structure on the distal end of the centriole that suppresses centriole elongation (Schmidt et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge and is supported by a citation to Schmidt et al., 2009, which is a reference to prior published work.

claim: CP110 forms a cap-like structure on the distal end of the centriole that suppresses centriole elongation.
source: Centrobin is further required to recruit CP110, a protein forming a cap-like structure on the distal end of the centriole that suppresses centriole elongation (Schmidt et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge and is supported by a citation to Schmidt et al., 2009, which is a reference to prior published work.

claim: POC5, POC1B, and OFD1 have been implicated in promoting the elongation of the centriole's distal region.
source: Proximal to CP110, several proteins localized to the distal luminal end of centrioles such as POC5 (Azimzadeh et al., 2009), POC1B (Venoux et al., 2013), and OFD1 (Singla et al., 2010) have been implicated in promoting the elongation of the centriole's distal region.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge and is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: CEP295 and RTTN have been proposed to play a scaffolding role in the elongation process by connecting the centriole wall to the luminal centriolar region.
source: More recently, additional proteins have been identified, namely CEP295 (Chang et al., 2016) and RTTN (Chen et al., 2017), which have been proposed to play a scaffolding role in the elongation process by connecting the centriole wall to the luminal centriolar region.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge and is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: RTTN was originally identified as a protein critical for axial rotation and left-right symmetry specification in mice.
source: RTTN (rotatin) was originally identified as a protein critical for axial rotation and left-right symmetry specification in mice (Faisst et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Faisst et al., 2002, which is a reference to prior published work.

claim: The Drosophila RTTN homolog, Ana3, was demonstrated to be a centrosomal component critical for maintaining the structural integrity of centrioles.
source: The Drosophila RTTN homolog, Ana3, was demonstrated to be a centrosomal component critical for maintaining the structural integrity of centrioles (Stevens et al., 2009), whereas human RTTN, localized near the centriolar cartwheel, has been shown to be dispensable for initial centriole assembly, but critical for formation of a full-length centriole (Chen et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Stevens et al., 2009, which is a reference to prior published work.

claim: Human RTTN is localized near the centriolar cartwheel.
source: The Drosophila RTTN homolog, Ana3, was demonstrated to be a centrosomal component critical for maintaining the structural integrity of centrioles (Stevens et al., 2009), whereas human RTTN, localized near the centriolar cartwheel, has been shown to be dispensable for initial centriole assembly, but critical for formation of a full-length centriole (Chen et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2017, which is a reference to prior published work.

claim: Human RTTN is dispensable for initial centriole assembly, but critical for formation of a full-length centriole.
source: The Drosophila RTTN homolog, Ana3, was demonstrated to be a centrosomal component critical for maintaining the structural integrity of centrioles (Stevens et al., 2009), whereas human RTTN, localized near the centriolar cartwheel, has been shown to be dispensable for initial centriole assembly, but critical for formation of a full-length centriole (Chen et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2017, which is a reference to prior published work.

claim: PPP1R35 is likely the human homolog of the Drosophila protein Reduction of Cnn dots 4 (Rcd4).
source: Our phylogenetic analysis demonstrates that PPP1R35 is conserved in a wide range of species, including Drosophila, parasitic worms, and mammals (Figure 5—figure supplement 1). PPP1R35 is likely the human homolog of the Drosophila protein Reduction of Cnn dots 4 (Rcd4), a protein identified in a large RNAi screen aimed at discovering novel proteins impacting centrosome formation and PCM assembly (Dobbelaere et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is inferred from phylogenetic analysis and is supported by a citation to Dobbelaere et al., 2008, which is a reference to prior published work.

claim: Rcd4 was identified in a large RNAi screen aimed at discovering novel proteins impacting centrosome formation and PCM assembly.
source: PPP1R35 is likely the human homolog of the Drosophila protein Reduction of Cnn dots 4 (Rcd4), a protein identified in a large RNAi screen aimed at discovering novel proteins impacting centrosome formation and PCM assembly (Dobbelaere et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Dobbelaere et al., 2008, which is a reference to prior published work.

claim: Alignment of Homo sapiens PPP1R35 and Drosophila Rcd4 results in an overall similarity of 24%, with the greatest homology in the conserved C-terminal domain.
source: Alignment of Homo sapiens PPP1R35 and Drosophila Rcd4 results in an overall similarity of 24%, with the greatest homology in the conserved C-terminal domain (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The conserved serines and putative PP1-binding site in PPP1R35, which are well conserved in Chordata, are not conserved in Rcd4.
source: Intriguingly, the aforementioned serines and putative PP1-binding site, which are well conserved in Chordata, are not conserved in Rcd4.
evidence: The claim is inferred from sequence alignment analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Changes to the phosphorylation state of PPP1R35 altered the overall BioID proximity map, including altering the proximity to CEP85, AZI1, and OFD1.

evidence: The claim is supported by BioID experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: AZI1 and OFD1 have important roles in ciliogenesis.
source: Furthermore, changes to the phosphorylation state did alter the overall BioID proximity map of PPP1R35, including altering the proximity to CEP85, AZI1, and OFD1, the latter two shown to have important roles in ciliogenesis (Hall et al., 2013; Ma and Jarman, 2011; Wilkinson et al., 2009; Romio et al., 2004; Ferrante et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge and is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: The centrosomal duplication cycle is closely linked to the cell cycle and tightly controlled by a host of kinases and phosphatases.
source: The centrosomal duplication cycle is closely linked to the cell cycle and tightly controlled by a host of kinases and phosphatases (Pihan, 2013; Fujita et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge and is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Protein phosphatases require a regulatory component to properly function.
source: While kinases inherently possess temporal and spatial specificity, protein phosphatases require a regulatory component to properly function (Heroes et al., 2013; Peti et al., 2013; Korrodi-Gregório et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge and is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Only a handful of centrosomal PP1 regulatory components have been identified to date.
source: To date, only a handful of centrosomal PP1 regulatory components have been identified (Katayama et al., 2001; Meraldi and Nigg, 2001; Mi et al., 2007; Helps et al., 2000; DeVaul et al., 2013; Huang et al., 2005) and overall knowledge of their interaction and role with PP1 is limited in scope.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge and is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: PPP1R35 is annotated to be a PP1-regulatory protein and contains a canonical PP1-binding site.
source: PPP1R35 is annotated to be a PP1-regulatory protein and contains a canonical PP1-binding site.
evidence: The claim is based on established annotation and sequence analysis.

claim: Previous reports demonstrated PP1-binding and inhibition by PPP1R35.
source: Despite previous reports that demonstrated PP1-binding and inhibition (Hendrickx et al., 2009; Fardilha et al., 2011), we were unable to identify any PP1 isoform in our BioID or IP screens using HEK293 cycling cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hendrickx et al., 2009 and Fardilha et al., 2011, which are references to prior published work.

claim: No PP1 isoform was identified in BioID or IP screens of PPP1R35 using HEK293 cycling cells.
source: Despite previous reports that demonstrated PP1-binding and inhibition (Hendrickx et al., 2009; Fardilha et al., 2011), we were unable to identify any PP1 isoform in our BioID or IP screens using HEK293 cycling cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by BioID and IP experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The PP1-regulating activity of PPP1R35 may not be related to centriole biogenesis.
source: Overall, this suggests that despite PPP1R35's annotation and previous demonstration as a PP1 regulator, this activity may not be related to centriole biogenesis.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that the PP1-binding site is not critical for centriole biogenesis.

claim: PPP1R35 may serve other functions in the cell apart from centriole duplication.
source: Nonetheless, the large number of robust, non-centrosomal BioID hits suggests that PPP1R35 may serve other functions in the cell apart from centriole duplication and perhaps these other functions require PPP1R35's PP1-regulation activity.
evidence: The claim is speculative and is inferred from the observation of non-centrosomal BioID hits.

claim: Two major pathways governing centriole elongation have been described: one positive-growth mechanism acting on assisting microtubule elongation (CPAP/CEP120/SPICE) and a second negative-growth mechanism involving CP110 and CEP97.
source: To date, two major pathways governing centriole elongation have been described, one positive-growth mechanism acting on assisting microtubule elongation (CPAP/CEP120/SPICE) (Kohlmaier et al., 2009; Schmidt et al., 2009; Tang et al., 2009; Lin et al., 2013b; Comartin et al., 2013) and a second negative-growth mechanism involving CP110 and CEP97, which form a cap-like structure on the centriole to restrict microtubule growth (Schmidt et al., 2009; Spektor et al., 2007; Franz et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge and is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: CP110 and CEP97 form a cap-like structure on the centriole to restrict microtubule growth.
source: To date, two major pathways governing centriole elongation have been described, one positive-growth mechanism acting on assisting microtubule elongation (CPAP/CEP120/SPICE) (Kohlmaier et al., 2009; Schmidt et al., 2009; Tang et al., 2009; Lin et al., 2013b; Comartin et al., 2013) and a second negative-growth mechanism involving CP110 and CEP97, which form a cap-like structure on the centriole to restrict microtubule growth (Schmidt et al., 2009; Spektor et al., 2007; Franz et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge and is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: PPP1R35 primarily impacts the CPAP/CEP120/SPICE and RTTN/CEP295 pathways of centriole elongation.
source: Our data suggest that PPP1R35 primarily impacts the CPAP/CEP120/SPICE and RTTN/CEP295 pathways of centriole elongation (Figure 6d,e).
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data presented in the manuscript and is summarized in Figure 6d,e.

claim: RTTN was proposed to be critical for stabilizing the early procentriole containing STIL, CPAP, and SAS6 and for recruiting CEP295.
source: Previously, RTTN was proposed to be critical for stabilizing the early procentriole containing STIL, CPAP, and SAS6 and for recruiting CEP295, which in turn can recruit POC5 and POC1B (Chen et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2017, which is a reference to prior published work.

claim: CEP295 can recruit POC5 and POC1B.
source: Previously, RTTN was proposed to be critical for stabilizing the early procentriole containing STIL, CPAP, and SAS6 and for recruiting CEP295, which in turn can recruit POC5 and POC1B (Chen et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2017, which is a reference to prior published work.

claim: The impact of PPP1R35 on centriole elongation occurs primarily through PPP1R35's interaction with RTTN.
source: Our data are consistent with a model where the impact on centriole elongation occurs primarily through PPP1R35's interaction with RTTN.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: PPP1R35 could be involved in either modulating RTTN's turnover or interactions with other proteins.
source: PPP1R35 could be involved in either modulating RTTN's turnover or interactions with other proteins.
evidence: The claim is speculative and is based on inference from the observed interaction between PPP1R35 and RTTN.

claim: RTTN loss causes lack of proper CEP295, POC1B, and POC5 recruitment and an interdependency with CPAP and CEP135.
source: This reasoning is supported by the observation that RTTN loss has been shown to cause lack of proper CEP295, POC1B, and POC5 recruitment and an interdependency with CPAP and CEP135 (Chen et al., 2017), consistent with our observed phenotype when PPP1R35 is knocked down.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2017, which is a reference to prior published work.

claim: Mutations in CPAP cause microcephaly.
source: Mutations in numerous centriolar proteins have been linked to microcephaly (Barbelanne and Tsang, 2014; Kaindl et al., 2010), including components involved in centriole elongation such as CPAP (Leal et al., 2003) and RTTN (Care4Rare Canada Consortium et al., 2015; Grandone et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Leal et al., 2003, which is a reference to prior published work.

claim: PPP1R35 may be a candidate microcephaly gene.
source: Our data show that that PPP1R35 impacts the process of centriole elongation through a close relationship with a known microcephaly protein, RTTN, therefore suggesting that PPP1R35 may be one such candidate microcephaly gene.
evidence: The claim is speculative and is inferred from the observed relationship between PPP1R35 and RTTN.

claim: Tubulin acetylation is unaffected when PPP1R35 is knocked down by siRNA.
source: Furthermore, we verified that tubulin acetylation is unaffected when PPP1R35 is knocked down by siRNA (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Acetylated tubulin has been suggested to be an early tubulin modification during centriole duplication.
source: Acetylated tubulin has been suggested to be an early tubulin modification during centriole duplication (Balashova et al., 2009) and it has been previously used for conducting centriole length measurements (Chen et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Balashova et al., 2009 and Chen et al., 2017, which are references to prior published work.

claim: Acetylated tubulin has been previously used for conducting centriole length measurements.
source: Acetylated tubulin has been suggested to be an early tubulin modification during centriole duplication (Balashova et al., 2009) and it has been previously used for conducting centriole length measurements (Chen et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2017, which is a reference to prior published work.
